prompt: Which command creates a new, empty Git repository in the current directory?
options: git init
git start
git new
git create
optionNotes: `git init` creates a `.git` directory with an empty object database and refs, turning the current directory into a repository, which is exactly what the prompt asks for.
`git start` is not a Git command; Git has no subcommand by that name.
`git new` is not a built-in Git command; repository creation is done with `git init` (or `git clone` for existing repos).
`git create` does not exist in Git; some hosting CLIs like `gh repo create` create remote repos, but that is not part of Git itself.
explanation: `git init` creates a new `.git` subdirectory, turning the current directory into a Git repository. The other commands are not real Git commands.
example:
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
git init   # creates the .git directory
git status # 'No commits yet'
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["Plain directory"] -->|"git init"| B["Creates .git subdirectory"]
B --> C["Empty repository"]
C --> D["No commits yet"]
D -->|"git add + git commit"| E["First commit"]

prompt: Which command moves changes from the working directory into the staging area (index) so they will be included in the next commit?
options: git commit
git index
git add
git track
optionNotes: `git commit` records what is already in the index as a commit; it does not itself move working-tree changes into the staging area (except with `-a`, which stages tracked files as a shortcut).
`git index` is not a Git command; the index is the internal name for the staging area, but you interact with it through `git add`, `git reset` and `git restore --staged`.
`git add` copies the current content of files from the working directory into the index so it will be part of the next commit, which is precisely the staging step.
`git track` is not a Git command; tracking begins the first time a file is added with `git add`.
explanation: `git add <file>` stages changes (`git stage` is an accepted synonym). `git index` and `git track` are not Git commands, and `git commit` records already-staged changes rather than staging new ones.
example:
git add src/app.py        # stage one file
git add -A                # stage all changes
git add -p                # interactively stage hunks
diagram:
flowchart LR
W["Working directory (edited files)"] -->|"git add file"| S["Staging area (index)"]
S -->|"git commit"| R["Repository (history)"]
N["git stage = synonym of git add"] --> S

prompt: Which command shows which files are staged, unstaged, or untracked in the working directory?
options: git diff
git status
git log
git show
optionNotes: `git diff` shows line-level changes between the working tree and index (or between commits); it does not give the per-file staged/unstaged/untracked summary.
`git status` reports the state of the working tree and index, listing staged, unstaged, and untracked files, which is what the prompt describes.
`git log` lists commit history; it says nothing about the current state of the working directory.
`git show` displays an object such as a commit with its diff; it does not summarise the working directory state.
explanation: `git status` summarizes the state of the working directory and staging area. `git diff` shows line-by-line changes, and `git log` shows commit history.
example:
git status
# On branch main
# Changes to be committed:   modified: README.md
# Changes not staged:        modified: app.py
# Untracked files:           notes.txt
git status -s   # short form
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git status"] --> B["Staged changes (ready to commit)"]
A --> C["Unstaged changes (modified, not added)"]
A --> D["Untracked files (never added)"]
E["git diff shows line changes"] -.-> C
F["git log shows commit history"] -.-> G["Not working tree state"]

prompt: Which command records the currently staged snapshot as a new commit in the repository history?
options: git save
git push
git commit
git checkout
optionNotes: `git save` is not a Git command; there is no such subcommand.
`git push` uploads existing local commits to a remote; it does not create commits from the staging area.
`git commit` takes the contents of the index and stores them as a new commit object with a message and parent, which is what the prompt asks.
`git checkout` switches branches or restores files in the working tree; it does not record a commit.
explanation: `git commit` creates a new commit from whatever is currently staged. `git push` sends commits to a remote, and `git save` is not a Git command.
example:
git add .
git commit -m "Add login endpoint"   # records the staged snapshot
git commit                          # opens editor for the message
diagram:
flowchart LR
S["Staging area snapshot"] -->|"git commit -m msg"| C["New commit object"]
C --> H["Branch / HEAD moves to it"]
H -->|"git push (later)"| R["Remote repository"]
X["git save = not a Git command"] -.-> S

prompt: Which command displays the commit history for the current branch?
options: git log
git history
git track
git commits
optionNotes: `git log` walks backward from HEAD and prints each commit's hash, author, date, and message, which is the commit history for the current branch.
`git history` is not a built-in Git command.
`git track` does not exist in Git.
`git commits` is not a Git command; history is viewed with `git log`.
explanation: `git log` lists commits reachable from HEAD, newest first by default. `git history`, `git track`, and `git commits` are not Git commands.
example:
git log                 # full history of the current branch
git log --oneline -5    # last 5 commits, one per line
git log --graph --all   # visualise all branches
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["git log"] --> H["HEAD"]
H --> C3["commit c3 (newest)"]
C3 --> C2["commit c2"]
C2 --> C1["commit c1 (oldest)"]
N["Lists commits reachable from HEAD, newest first"] -.-> A

prompt: What is the purpose of a `.gitignore` file?
options: It lists files and directories that Git should not track or stage
It stores commit messages for reuse
It configures the remote repository URL
It lists branches that cannot be deleted
optionNotes: A `.gitignore` file contains patterns for paths that Git should treat as intentionally untracked, so they are not shown as untracked or staged by `git add`; this is its purpose.
Commit messages are not stored in `.gitignore`; message templates use `commit.template` and reusable text is not a Git feature of this file.
Remote URLs are configured in `.git/config` via `git remote`; `.gitignore` has nothing to do with remotes.
Branch deletion restrictions are enforced by server-side branch protection, not by `.gitignore`.
explanation: `.gitignore` contains patterns matching files Git should leave untracked, such as build artifacts or secrets, so they never get accidentally staged.
example:
# .gitignore
node_modules/
*.log
.env
dist/
# Then: git status no longer lists these paths as untracked
diagram:
flowchart TD
F[".gitignore patterns (node_modules, *.log, .env)"] --> M{"Does file match?"}
M -->|"yes"| I["Ignored: never staged by git add"]
M -->|"no"| T["Shown as untracked, can be staged"]
I --> S["Secrets and build artifacts stay out of history"]

prompt: Which command switches your working directory to an existing branch named `develop`?
options: git branch develop
git switch develop
git merge develop
git fetch develop
optionNotes: `git branch develop` creates a new branch named develop at HEAD (or errors if it exists); it does not change which branch is checked out.
`git switch develop` updates HEAD and the working tree to the existing develop branch, which is what the prompt asks for; `git checkout develop` does the same.
`git merge develop` integrates develop's commits into the current branch; it does not switch branches.
`git fetch develop` would try to fetch from a remote named develop; it does not change the checked-out branch.
explanation: `git switch develop` (or the older `git checkout develop`) changes the currently checked-out branch. `git branch develop` only creates a branch without switching to it.
example:
git switch develop       # switch to existing branch
git checkout develop     # older equivalent
git switch -c feature/x  # create and switch
diagram:
flowchart LR
M["On branch main"] -->|"git switch develop"| D["On branch develop (HEAD moved)"]
M -->|"git checkout develop (older form)"| D
M -->|"git branch develop"| C["Creates branch only, HEAD stays on main"]

prompt: You run `git branch -d old-feature` and it fails with an error saying the branch is not fully merged. What does this tell you?
options: The branch contains commits that are not reachable from your current branch's history, so Git refuses to delete it to avoid losing work
The branch name is invalid
You must first push the branch to a remote before deleting it
Git never allows deleting local branches
optionNotes: The lowercase `-d` flag only deletes branches whose commits are already reachable from the current branch (or upstream); the error means unmerged commits exist and Git is protecting them, so this is the right reading.
An invalid branch name yields a different error such as 'branch not found'; the not-fully-merged message specifically concerns unmerged commits.
Git never requires pushing before local deletion; the safety check is about local reachability, not remotes.
Git does allow deleting local branches with `-d` (when merged) or `-D` (force), so this claim is false.
explanation: `-d` is the safe delete flag: Git refuses if deleting the branch would make commits unreachable. Using `-D` forces deletion regardless.
example:
git branch -d old-feature
# error: The branch 'old-feature' is not fully merged.
git log main..old-feature   # see the unmerged commits
git branch -D old-feature   # force delete if you really mean it
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git branch -d old-feature"] --> Q{"All commits reachable from current branch?"}
Q -->|"yes"| B["Branch deleted safely"]
Q -->|"no"| C["Error: branch not fully merged"]
C --> D["Commits would become unreachable"]
C -->|"really discard?"| E["git branch -D forces deletion"]

prompt: What is a 'fast-forward' merge?
options: A merge where the current branch's pointer is simply moved forward to the target commit because no divergent commits exist on the current branch
A merge that automatically resolves all conflicts
A merge performed with the `--force` flag
A merge that squashes all commits into one before merging
optionNotes: When the current branch has no commits that the target lacks, Git simply advances the branch ref to the target commit without creating a merge commit; this is the definition of a fast-forward.
No merge type automatically resolves all conflicts; a fast-forward simply cannot have conflicts because nothing diverged.
`--force` is not a `git merge` option; forcing relates to `git push --force` or `git branch -f`, not fast-forward merges.
Squashing is done with `git merge --squash`, which is a separate behaviour that collapses commits; it is unrelated to fast-forwarding.
explanation: A fast-forward happens when the current branch has no commits of its own since it diverged, so Git can just move the branch pointer forward instead of creating a merge commit.
example:
git switch main
git merge feature
# Updating a1b2c3d..e4f5g6h
# Fast-forward
git merge --no-ff feature   # force a merge commit instead
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["c1"] --> B["c2 (main before merge)"]
B --> C["c3 (feature)"]
C --> D["c4 (feature tip)"]
B -.->|"main has no new commits"| E["git merge feature"]
E --> F["main pointer moves to c4, no merge commit"]

prompt: Compared to `git merge`, what does `git rebase` do to integrate changes from one branch onto another?
options: It replays your branch's commits one by one on top of the target branch, producing a linear history without a merge commit
It deletes the commits from the other branch
It only works on remote branches, never local ones
It automatically squashes every commit into a single commit
optionNotes: `git rebase` takes the commits unique to your branch and re-applies them one at a time onto the tip of the target branch, producing new commits and a linear history with no merge commit.
Rebase does not delete commits from the other branch; the target branch is untouched and only your branch's commits are rewritten.
Rebase works on any local branch; it is commonly run entirely locally before pushing.
Plain rebase preserves each commit separately; squashing only happens if you choose it in an interactive rebase (`-i`).
explanation: Rebase re-applies each commit from your branch onto the tip of the target branch, resulting in a linear history instead of the merge commit that `git merge` would create.
example:
git switch feature
git rebase main      # replay feature commits on top of main
# resolve conflicts, then:
git rebase --continue
git log --oneline --graph   # linear history
diagram:
flowchart LR
subgraph merge["git merge"]
M1["main tip"] --> MC["merge commit (2 parents)"]
F1["feature tip"] --> MC
end
subgraph rebase["git rebase main"]
R1["main tip"] --> R2["feature c1 replayed"]
R2 --> R3["feature c2 replayed"]
R3 --> L["linear history, new hashes"]
end

prompt: During a merge conflict, what do the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers in a file indicate?
options: They separate the conflicting content from your current branch and the branch being merged in
They mark lines that Git has permanently deleted
They indicate syntax errors unrelated to the merge
They are automatically removed and can be ignored
optionNotes: Git writes the conflicting hunk with the current branch's version between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` and the incoming branch's version between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`, so you can choose or combine them manually.
Nothing is permanently deleted; both versions are preserved inside the markers until you resolve the conflict.
The markers are inserted by Git during a merge, not by a language parser, although leaving them in will usually cause syntax errors.
They are never removed automatically; you must edit the file, remove the markers, and stage it to complete the merge.
explanation: Git inserts these markers around the conflicting sections: content above `=======` comes from your current branch (HEAD), content below comes from the branch being merged in. You must edit the file to resolve them.
example:
<<<<<<< HEAD
port = 8080
=======
port = 9090
>>>>>>> feature/ports
# keep the wanted lines, delete the markers, then: git add config.py && git commit
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["<<<<<<< HEAD"] --> B["Content from your current branch"]
B --> C["======="]
C --> D["Content from branch being merged"]
D --> E[">>>>>>> other-branch"]
E --> F["Edit file, remove markers"]
F --> G["git add, then git commit"]

prompt: What is the key difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: `git fetch` only downloads remote history without changing your working branch, while `git pull` fetches and then merges (or rebases) into your current branch
`git fetch` uploads commits while `git pull` downloads them
There is no difference; they are aliases for the same command
`git pull` only works on the first clone of a repository
optionNotes: `git fetch` downloads objects and updates remote-tracking refs like `origin/main` without touching your branch, while `git pull` is fetch followed by merge or rebase into the current branch; this captures the real difference.
Uploading commits is done by `git push`; both fetch and pull download from the remote.
They are not aliases; `pull` literally runs `fetch` and then `merge` (or `rebase`).
`git pull` can be run at any time on any branch with an upstream, not only after the first clone.
explanation: `git pull` is effectively `git fetch` followed by `git merge` (or `git rebase` with `--rebase`). `git fetch` alone updates remote-tracking branches but never touches your local branches.
example:
git fetch origin            # update origin/main, working branch untouched
git log main..origin/main   # review what arrived
git merge origin/main       # integrate when ready
git pull --rebase origin main   # fetch + rebase in one step
diagram:
flowchart LR
R["Remote origin/main"] -->|"git fetch"| T["Updates remote-tracking ref origin/main only"]
T -.->|"local branch untouched"| L["Local main unchanged"]
R -->|"git pull"| P["fetch + merge (or rebase)"]
P --> M["Local main updated"]

prompt: Which command uploads your local commits on the current branch to a remote repository?
options: git push
git send
git upload
git commit --remote
optionNotes: `git push` transfers local commits and updates the corresponding branch on the remote, which is what the prompt asks.
`git send` is not a Git command; the closest is `git send-email`, which mails patches rather than pushing.
`git upload` does not exist; `git upload-pack` is an internal server-side helper, not a user command.
`git commit --remote` is not a valid option; `git commit` only records commits locally.
explanation: `git push` transfers local commits to a remote repository and updates the corresponding remote branch.
example:
git push                    # push current branch to its upstream
git push origin feature/x   # explicit remote and branch
git push --force-with-lease # safer force push after a rebase
diagram:
flowchart LR
W["Working dir"] -->|"git add"| S["Index"]
S -->|"git commit"| L["Local branch commits"]
L -->|"git push origin branch"| R["Remote branch updated"]
R -.->|"pull brings the other direction"| L

prompt: Fill in the missing command: to register a remote repository named `origin` pointing at `https://example.com/repo.git`, you would run: `___ origin https://example.com/repo.git`
explanation: Full command accepted too.
example:
git remote add origin https://example.com/repo.git
git remote -v   # verify: origin https://example.com/repo.git (fetch/push)
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["git remote add origin URL"] --> B["Writes remote origin into .git/config"]
B --> C["origin = https://example.com/repo.git"]
C -->|"git push origin main"| D["Upload commits"]
C -->|"git fetch origin"| E["Download commits"]
F["git remote -v lists remotes"] -.-> C

prompt: Fill in the command that pushes the current branch to `origin` and, in the same step, sets it as the upstream tracking branch.
explanation: The `-u`/`--set-upstream` flag on `git push` both pushes the branch and records the tracking relationship.
example:
git switch -c feature/login
git push -u origin HEAD          # push and set upstream
git push --set-upstream origin feature/login   # long form
git status   # 'Your branch is up to date with origin/feature/login'
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["git push -u origin HEAD"] --> B["Pushes current branch to origin"]
A --> C["Records upstream: branch tracks origin/branch"]
C --> D["Later: plain git push / git pull work without args"]
E["--set-upstream is the long form of -u"] -.-> A

prompt: What is the primary purpose of `git stash`?
options: To temporarily shelve uncommitted changes so you can switch context (e.g. branches) and reapply them later
To permanently delete uncommitted changes
To create a backup branch automatically on every commit
To compress the `.git` repository to save disk space
optionNotes: `git stash` saves the working tree and index changes into a stash entry and restores a clean working tree, so you can switch branches and later `pop` or `apply` them; this is its primary purpose.
Stashed changes are stored in the repository, not deleted; permanent removal would be `git stash drop` or `git checkout -- .`.
Git does not create backup branches on commit; the reflog is the closest safety mechanism.
Repository compression is done by `git gc`; `git stash` does not affect disk usage of the object store.
explanation: `git stash` saves your uncommitted working directory and index changes on a stack, restoring a clean working directory so you can do something else, then reapply the changes later with `git stash pop` or `git stash apply`.
example:
git stash            # shelve uncommitted changes
git switch hotfix    # do other work
git switch feature
git stash pop        # bring the changes back
git stash list       # see saved stashes
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["Uncommitted changes in working dir"] -->|"git stash"| B["Saved on stash stack"]
B --> C["Clean working directory"]
C -->|"git switch other-branch, do work"| D["Come back"]
D -->|"git stash pop / apply"| E["Changes reapplied"]

prompt: You can have more than one stash entry saved at the same time, and `git stash list` will show all of them.
explanation: `git stash` pushes each stash onto a stack, so multiple stashes can coexist; `git stash list` shows them all, most recent first.
example:
git stash push -m "wip: header"
git stash push -m "wip: footer"
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On main: wip: footer
# stash@{1}: On main: wip: header
git stash apply stash@{1}
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git stash (edit A)"] --> S0["stash@{2}"]
B["git stash (edit B)"] --> S1["stash@{1}"]
C["git stash (edit C)"] --> S2["stash@{0} most recent"]
L["git stash list shows all three"] --> S2
L --> S1
L --> S0

prompt: What does `git reset --soft HEAD~1` do?
options: Moves the branch pointer back one commit, but leaves the index and working directory unchanged, so the previous commit's changes appear staged
Deletes the last commit's changes from disk permanently
Moves the branch pointer back one commit and unstages the changes, but keeps them in the working directory
Discards all local commits and matches the remote
optionNotes: With `--soft`, only the branch ref moves; the index still holds the previous commit's tree, so its changes show as staged and the working directory is untouched.
Nothing is deleted from disk by a soft reset; both index and working tree are preserved.
Unstaging while keeping working-tree changes describes `--mixed` (the default), not `--soft`.
Discarding local commits to match the remote would be `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`, not a soft reset of one commit.
explanation: `--soft` only moves HEAD (and the branch ref); the index and working tree are untouched, so the changes from the undone commit remain staged and ready to be recommitted.
example:
git reset --soft HEAD~1   # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git status                # 'Changes to be committed'
git commit -m "Better message"   # re-commit
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["git reset --soft HEAD~1"] --> H["HEAD and branch move back one commit"]
A --> I["Index unchanged: changes still staged"]
A --> W["Working tree unchanged"]
I -->|"git commit"| R["Recommit the same changes"]

prompt: What does `git reset --mixed HEAD~1` (the default mode of `git reset`) do?
options: Moves the branch pointer back one commit and resets the index to match, but leaves working directory files unchanged
Moves the branch pointer back and also deletes working directory changes
Only updates the working directory, leaving the index untouched
Creates a new commit that undoes the previous one
optionNotes: The mixed mode moves the branch ref and resets the index to that commit, but leaves the working directory files as they are, so the changes appear unstaged.
Deleting working-directory changes is what `--hard` does; `--mixed` keeps them.
Updating only the working directory is not a reset mode; `--mixed` always updates the index.
Creating a new undo commit is `git revert`, not `git reset`.
explanation: `--mixed` is the default: it moves HEAD and resets the staging area to match the new HEAD, but working directory files are left as-is, so changes appear as unstaged modifications.
example:
git reset HEAD~1          # same as --mixed
git status                # changes now unstaged but still in files
git add -p && git commit  # re-stage selectively
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["git reset --mixed HEAD~1 (default)"] --> H["HEAD moves back one commit"]
A --> I["Index reset to match new HEAD"]
A --> W["Working tree files kept"]
I --> U["Changes now appear unstaged"]
U -->|"git add"| S["Stage again if wanted"]

prompt: Why is `git reset --hard` considered dangerous?
options: It moves the branch pointer and overwrites both the index and the working directory, permanently discarding any uncommitted changes
It permanently deletes the remote repository
It rewrites the history of every branch in the repository
It disables the ability to ever commit again
optionNotes: `--hard` resets the branch ref, the index, and the working directory to the target commit, so any uncommitted edits are overwritten and cannot be recovered via reflog.
`git reset` only affects the local repository; it never touches or deletes a remote.
It only moves the current branch's ref, not every branch in the repository.
Committing is still possible afterwards; the danger is data loss, not a disabled command.
explanation: `--hard` resets HEAD, the index, and the working directory to match the target commit, discarding uncommitted work with no confirmation. Committed work may still be recoverable via the reflog, but uncommitted changes are generally lost.
example:
git reset --hard HEAD~1   # uncommitted edits are gone for good
# safer alternatives:
git stash                 # save first
git reflog                # can recover committed work, not uncommitted
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git reset --hard target"] --> H["HEAD moves"]
A --> I["Index overwritten"]
A --> W["Working tree overwritten"]
W --> L["Uncommitted changes lost, no confirmation"]
H -.->|"committed work"| R["Still recoverable via git reflog"]

prompt: Why is `git revert` generally preferred over `git reset` for undoing a commit that has already been pushed and shared with others?
options: `git revert` creates a new commit that undoes the changes, preserving history, while `git reset` rewrites history which can break other collaborators' clones
`git revert` is faster to type
`git reset` only works on remote branches
`git revert` cannot undo merge commits
optionNotes: `git revert` adds a new commit that inverts the change, so shared history is not rewritten, while `git reset` moves the branch pointer and requires a force push that breaks others' clones.
Typing speed is irrelevant; the preference is about preserving shared history.
`git reset` operates on local branches; it is not limited to remote branches.
`git revert` can undo merge commits using `-m <parent-number>`, so this is not a reason to prefer it.
explanation: Because `revert` adds a new commit instead of removing or rewriting existing ones, it is safe to use on shared branches. `reset` moves the branch pointer and, if the rewritten history is pushed, forces collaborators to reconcile diverged histories.
example:
git revert abc1234        # new commit that undoes abc1234
git push                  # history only grows, collaborators fast-forward
# versus: git reset --hard HEAD~1 && git push --force  (rewrites shared history)
diagram:
flowchart LR
subgraph revert["git revert (safe on shared)"]
A["c1"] --> B["c2 bad"]
B --> C["c3 inverse of c2"]
end
subgraph reset["git reset (rewrites)"]
D["c1"] --> E["c2 removed from branch"]
E --> F["Force push needed, collaborators diverge"]
end

prompt: Running `git revert <commit>` deletes the target commit from the repository's history.
explanation: `git revert` does not remove or rewrite the original commit; it creates a brand new commit that applies the inverse of the target commit's changes, keeping full history intact.
example:
git revert abc1234
git log --oneline -2
# 9f8e7d6 Revert "Add feature X"
# abc1234 Add feature X   <- still present
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["c1"] --> B["c2 (target)"]
B --> C["c3"]
C -->|"git revert c2"| D["c4 = inverse diff of c2"]
B -.->|"still in history"| N["Not deleted or rewritten"]

prompt: What does `git cherry-pick <commit>` do?
options: Applies the changes introduced by a specific commit from another branch onto the current branch as a new commit
Deletes a commit from the current branch
Merges two entire branches together
Lists commits that have not yet been pushed
optionNotes: `git cherry-pick` computes the diff introduced by the given commit and applies it to the current branch as a new commit with a new hash; this is its definition.
Cherry-pick never deletes commits; removing one from history would be `git rebase -i` and `drop`.
Merging whole branches is `git merge`; cherry-pick works one commit (or range) at a time.
Listing unpushed commits is `git log @{u}..` or `git cherry`, not `git cherry-pick`.
explanation: `cherry-pick` takes the diff introduced by one specific commit and applies it to the current branch, creating a new commit with (by default) a new hash.
example:
git switch main
git cherry-pick abc1234       # new commit on main with abc1234's changes
git cherry-pick -x abc1234    # add '(cherry picked from commit ...)' to message
diagram:
flowchart LR
F1["feature: c1"] --> F2["feature: c2 (wanted)"]
F2 --> F3["feature: c3"]
M1["main: m1"] --> M2["main: m2"]
F2 -->|"git cherry-pick c2"| M3["main: c2' (new hash)"]
M2 --> M3

prompt: A `git cherry-pick` can fail with a conflict, in which case you must resolve it manually and then run `git cherry-pick --continue`, just as you would during a rebase.
explanation: Cherry-picking replays a commit's diff onto a potentially different tree, so conflicts can occur. Git pauses and lets you resolve files, `git add` them, and then run `git cherry-pick --continue` (or `--abort` to cancel).
example:
git cherry-pick abc1234
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.py
vim app.py            # resolve markers
git add app.py
git cherry-pick --continue
# or abandon: git cherry-pick --abort
diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
[*] --> Applying: git cherry-pick commit
Applying --> Done: no conflict
Applying --> Conflict: overlapping changes
Conflict --> Resolved: edit files, git add
Resolved --> Done: git cherry-pick --continue
Conflict --> Aborted: git cherry-pick --abort
Done --> [*]

prompt: What is the main difference between a lightweight tag and an annotated tag in Git?

It lists every file ever tracked by the repository

prompt: What is the purpose of `git bisect`?
options: It performs a binary search through commit history, checking out candidate commits so you can mark each as good or bad, to quickly find the commit that introduced a bug
It splits a branch into two new branches at the current commit
It compares two branches and lists only the commits unique to each
It automatically bisects (halves) large files to reduce repository size
optionNotes: `git bisect` binary-searches between a known good and known bad commit, checking out midpoints for you to test, which finds the culprit in O(log n) steps; this is its purpose.
Splitting a branch is done by creating a new branch with `git branch`; bisect does not create branches.
Comparing unique commits between branches is `git log A...B --left-right` or `git cherry`, not bisect.
Bisect has nothing to do with file size; large files are handled by tools like Git LFS.
explanation: `git bisect` automates a binary search: you tell it one known-good and one known-bad commit, it checks out a midpoint, and you test and mark it good/bad, repeating until it narrows down the exact commit that introduced the regression.
example:
git bisect start
git bisect bad            # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.2.0    # known good release
# test, then mark: git bisect good | git bisect bad
git bisect reset          # done

A --> C["Merge base section, marked with pipes (diff3 only)"]

prompt: Fill in the `git blame` flag that ignores whitespace-only changes, so a reformatting commit is not shown as the last author of every re-indented line: `git blame ___ src/main.py`
explanation: `git blame -w` ignores whitespace when comparing lines. Combine it with `-M` (moved within a file) and `-C` (copied from other files) to attribute lines to their original author rather than to a mass reformat or move. `blame.ignoreRevsFile` can skip whole commits.
example:
git blame -w src/main.py
git blame -w -M -C src/main.py
# skip an entire reformat commit for every blame:
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

A["Reformat commit re-indents file"] --> B["git blame shows reformatter everywhere"]
A --> C["git blame -w ignores whitespace"]
C --> D["Original authors shown"]
E["-M and -C follow moves and copies"] -.-> D

prompt: `git merge -X ours feature` and `git merge -s ours feature` are equivalent: both produce a merge commit whose tree is identical to the current branch, discarding every change from `feature`.
explanation: False. `-X ours` is an option to the default `ort` strategy: it performs a normal merge and only resolves conflicting hunks in favour of the current side, keeping all non-conflicting changes from `feature`. `-s ours` is a separate strategy that ignores the other branch's content entirely and records a merge whose tree equals `HEAD`.
example:
git merge -X ours feature   # real merge; conflicts auto-resolved to our side
git merge -s ours feature   # tree == HEAD, feature's changes dropped, history joined
git merge -X theirs feature # conflicts resolved to feature's side
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git merge feature"] --> B["-X ours: ort strategy option"]
A --> C["-s ours: whole strategy"]
B --> D["Non-conflicting changes merged, conflicts take our side"]
C --> E["Result tree identical to HEAD, feature content ignored"]

prompt: `git describe` on your current commit prints `v2.4.0-17-g9fceb02`. How should this string be read?
options: HEAD is 17 commits after the annotated tag `v2.4.0`, and its abbreviated hash is `9fceb02`
HEAD is tagged `v2.4.0`, and 17 other branches contain commit `9fceb02`
Tag `v2.4.0` was created 17 days ago by a user whose name starts with `g`
HEAD is 17 commits before `v2.4.0`, meaning the tag is on a newer commit than the one checked out
optionNotes: Correct: the format is `<tag>-<commits since tag>-g<abbrev hash>`; the `g` prefix just marks it as a git hash.
If HEAD were exactly on the tag, `git describe` would print only `v2.4.0`; branch counts are not part of the output.
No time or author information is encoded; the middle number is a commit count.
`git describe` only looks backwards through ancestors, so the tag is always at or behind HEAD, never ahead.
explanation: `git describe` finds the nearest reachable tag and reports it, followed by the number of commits since that tag and the abbreviated hash prefixed with `g` (for git). By default only annotated tags are considered; add `--tags` to include lightweight ones. If HEAD is exactly on the tag, only the tag name is printed.
example:
git describe            # v2.4.0-17-g9fceb02
git describe --tags     # also consider lightweight tags
git describe --dirty    # appends -dirty when the worktree has changes
git describe --exact-match  # fails unless HEAD is tagged
diagram:
flowchart LR
T["v2.4.0 (annotated tag)"] --> C1["..."] --> C17["17 commits later"]
C17 --> H["HEAD = 9fceb02"]
H --> O["v2.4.0-17-g9fceb02"]
O --> P["tag - count since tag - g plus short hash"]

prompt: When a file is tracked by Git LFS, what does the Git repository itself store for that file?
options: A small pointer text file containing the object's SHA-256 OID and size, while the content is stored on an LFS server
A compressed copy of the file in a separate packfile that is excluded from clones by default
Nothing at all; LFS files are listed in `.gitignore` and shared through the LFS server only
A symbolic link to the file's location in the LFS cache directory under `.git/lfs`
optionNotes: Correct: the pointer is a tiny UTF-8 file with `version`, `oid`, and `size` lines; the clean and smudge filters swap it for real content.
LFS objects never enter Git's object database or packfiles; that is the whole point of the design.
The file is tracked and committed; it is the pointer that gets versioned, so history and diffs still record which version was used.
Git stores a regular blob (the pointer), not a symlink; `.git/lfs` is only a local cache.
explanation: Git LFS replaces large files in the repository with small text pointer files containing the object's SHA-256 OID and size. The real content lives on the LFS server and is downloaded by the LFS client during checkout, keeping clones small.
example:
git lfs install
git lfs track "*.iso"      # writes to .gitattributes
git add .gitattributes disk.iso && git commit -m "Add image"
git show HEAD:disk.iso
# version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1
# oid sha256:4d7a...
# size 734003200
diagram:
flowchart LR
A["disk.iso in working tree"] -->|"clean filter on git add"| B["Pointer file committed to Git"]
A --> C["Content uploaded to LFS server"]
B -->|"smudge filter on checkout"| D["Content downloaded from LFS"]
E[".gitattributes: filter=lfs"] -.-> A

prompt: Which of the following are valid places or mechanisms Git consults to decide that an untracked file should be ignored?
options: A `.gitignore` file in the repository, including ones in subdirectories
The per-repository file `.git/info/exclude`
The global file configured with `core.excludesFile`
Patterns listed in `.gitattributes` with the `ignore` attribute
Files marked with `git update-index --assume-unchanged`
optionNotes: Correct: `.gitignore` files are read from the directory of the file upward, with the closest file taking precedence.
Correct: `exclude` behaves like `.gitignore` but is never committed, ideal for editor and personal scratch files.
Correct: this applies across all repositories for one user, typically holding OS and editor junk patterns.
Wrong: there is no `ignore` attribute; `.gitattributes` controls line endings, diff, merge, and filters, not ignoring.
Wrong: `--assume-unchanged` only affects already tracked files and is a performance hint, not an ignore mechanism.
explanation: Git reads ignore patterns from `.gitignore` files in the working tree (committed and shared), `.git/info/exclude` (local to one clone), and the file named by `core.excludesFile` (per user, default `~/.config/git/ignore`). `.gitattributes` and `--assume-unchanged` are unrelated to ignoring untracked files.
example:
echo 'dist/' >> .gitignore                 # shared with the team
echo '.idea/' >> .git/info/exclude        # only this clone
git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global
git check-ignore -v dist/app.js            # shows which rule matched
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["Untracked file"] --> B[".gitignore in same dir or parent dirs"]
A --> C[".git/info/exclude (local only)"]
A --> D["core.excludesFile (per user)"]
B --> E["Deeper .gitignore overrides shallower"]
F["git check-ignore -v explains the match"] -.-> A

prompt: A developer committed `config/prod.env` containing a live AWS access key to the `payments` repo and pushed it to `origin/main` two hours ago. GitHub's secret scanning has already emailed the security team, and three other engineers have pulled `main` since. Which actions are required to actually contain this incident?
options: Revoke the exposed key in AWS and issue a new one immediately, before any history cleanup
Rewrite history to remove the file from every commit (for example `git filter-repo --path config/prod.env --invert-paths`) and force-push all affected branches and tags
Add `config/prod.env` to `.gitignore` and push a commit that deletes the file; the secret is then no longer in the repository
Tell everyone who pulled to re-clone (or hard-reset to the rewritten refs) and ask the hosting provider to run garbage collection so cached objects are purged
Run `git revert HEAD` on `main` so the key is undone without rewriting shared history
optionNotes: Correct: once pushed, the key must be treated as compromised no matter what happens to the repo; rotation is the only step that removes the risk.
Correct: removing the blob from all reachable history (filter-repo or BFG) plus a force push is how the secret leaves the repository itself.
Wrong: a deletion commit leaves the key in every previous commit; anyone can `git show <sha>:config/prod.env` or find it in the history.
Correct: local clones and server-side caches still hold the old objects; re-cloning and provider-side GC are needed so the blob is not re-pushed or served.
Wrong: a revert adds a new commit and keeps the original commit (and the key) fully reachable in history.
explanation: History rewriting alone does not help because the key has been readable for hours and copied into other clones, so rotation comes first. `git filter-repo` removes the blob from every commit, and after the force push every collaborator must reset or re-clone so their stale objects are not pushed back; the host also has to purge cached objects.
example:
# 1. rotate the credential in AWS first
# 2. scrub history
pip install git-filter-repo
git filter-repo --path config/prod.env --invert-paths
git remote add origin git@github.com:acme/payments.git
git push --force --all origin && git push --force --tags origin
# 3. everyone: git fetch && git reset --hard origin/main  (or re-clone)
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["Secret pushed to origin/main"] --> B["Rotate the key now"]
B --> C["git filter-repo removes blob from all commits"]
C --> D["Force push all branches and tags"]
D --> E["Collaborators reset or re-clone"]
D --> F["Provider purges cached objects"]
G["Delete commit or revert"] -.->|"key still in history"| A

prompt: You meant to start a branch for a new feature but forgot, and have just made three local commits directly on `main`. Nothing has been pushed yet, and `git status` shows `Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 3 commits`. You want those three commits on a new branch `feature/export` and `main` back in sync with the remote. Which sequence does this without losing work?
options: `git branch feature/export` then `git reset --hard origin/main` while still on `main`
`git switch -c feature/export` then `git rebase origin/main`
`git stash` then `git switch -c feature/export` then `git stash pop`
`git reset --hard origin/main` then `git switch -c feature/export` and `git cherry-pick HEAD~3..HEAD`
optionNotes: Correct: creating the branch first pins the three commits to a new ref, and the hard reset then moves only `main` back to the remote tip.
This creates the branch correctly, but `main` still points at the three commits; the rebase is a no-op and `main` remains ahead of origin.
`git stash` only saves uncommitted changes; the commits already exist and would stay on `main`, leaving nothing to stash.
Resetting first drops the commits from `main` before any branch points at them; `HEAD~3..HEAD` then refers to the wrong range and the commits are recoverable only via the reflog.
explanation: Commits are safe as long as some ref points at them, so the order matters: create `feature/export` at the current `HEAD` first, then reset `main` to `origin/main`. Doing the reset first orphans the commits until you dig them out of the reflog.
example:
git status
# On branch main
# Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 3 commits.
git branch feature/export        # new ref at current HEAD
git reset --hard origin/main     # main back to remote tip
git switch feature/export
git log --oneline origin/main..  # the 3 commits are here
diagram:
flowchart LR
O["origin/main"] --> C1["c1"] --> C2["c2"] --> C3["c3"]
C3 --> F["feature/export (new)"]
O --> M["main after reset --hard"]
S["Step 1: git branch feature/export"] -.-> F
T["Step 2: git reset --hard origin/main"] -.-> M

prompt: A colleague ran `git reset --hard HEAD~4` on their local `feature/billing` branch, thinking it would undo a single commit, and lost four commits of work that were never pushed. `git log` now shows none of them. They have not run `git gc` or anything else since. What is the best next step to get the commits back?
options: Run `git reflog`, find the entry from just before the reset (for example `HEAD@{1}`), and run `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` or `git branch recovered HEAD@{1}`
Run `git fsck --lost-found` and copy the dangling blobs out of `.git/lost-found/other/` into the working tree
Run `git pull origin feature/billing` so the remote copy restores the missing commits
Run `git revert HEAD~4..HEAD` to reapply the four commits on top of the current tip
optionNotes: Correct: the reset only moved the branch pointer; the commits still exist and the reflog records where `HEAD` was before the reset.
`fsck` can find unreachable objects, but here the commits are still recorded in the reflog, so this is a far more laborious and lossy route than needed.
The commits were never pushed, so the remote has nothing to give back; the pull would just report the branch is up to date.
`git revert` needs the commits to be reachable to revert them, and even then it would create inverse commits, not restore the lost ones.
explanation: `git reset --hard` rewrites the branch ref and working tree but does not delete commit objects. The reflog keeps a per-ref history of where `HEAD` and the branch pointed, so `HEAD@{1}` (the state before the reset) can be checked out or reset to directly.
example:
git reflog
# 3f9c2a1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~4
# b71e0d4 HEAD@{1}: commit: add invoice PDF export
# ...
git branch recovered b71e0d4      # or: git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
git log --oneline recovered -5
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git reset --hard HEAD~4"] --> B["Branch ref moves back 4 commits"]
B --> C["Commits still in object store"]
C --> D["git reflog lists HEAD@{1} = pre-reset tip"]
D --> E["git reset --hard HEAD@{1}"]
D --> F["or git branch recovered HEAD@{1}"]

prompt: During a release, a teammate ran `git push --force origin main` after a botched rebase, and the server-side branch `main` now points at commit `a1b2c3d`. Two commits that another engineer had pushed to `main` in the previous hour are gone from the remote. The teammate's own clone never fetched those two commits. Which action recovers them most directly?
options: Ask the engineer who authored the two commits to `git push origin main` again from their clone, which still has them, after merging or rebasing onto the new `main`
Run `git reflog origin/main` in the teammate's clone to find the previous remote tip and force-push it back
Run `git revert a1b2c3d` on `main` to undo the force push
Ask the hosting provider to restore the repository from last night's backup
optionNotes: Correct: any clone that fetched the commits (the author's most of all) still holds them and can push them back; hosting-side reflogs or event logs are a fallback if no clone has them.
Local reflogs only record what that clone saw; this clone never fetched the two commits, so `origin/main`'s reflog has no entry pointing at them.
`revert` undoes the changes of a commit; it cannot bring back commits that are no longer reachable from any ref.
A backup restore would also discard everything else pushed since the backup and is a last resort, not the most direct fix.
explanation: A force push only moves the remote ref; commits are lost from the remote's reachability, not from every clone. The fastest recovery is to find a clone that still has them (the author's, a CI runner, or a colleague who pulled) and push them back, then protect `main` against force pushes.
example:
# on the author's machine
git fetch origin
git log --oneline origin/main..main   # shows the 2 missing commits
git rebase origin/main               # or merge
git push origin main
# afterwards: enable 'block force pushes' on main in the host's branch protection
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git push --force origin main"] --> B["Remote main now at a1b2c3d"]
B --> C["2 commits unreachable on remote"]
C --> D{"Any clone still has them?"}
D -->|"author's clone"| E["rebase onto new main and push"]
D -->|"none"| F["Host reflog or support ticket"]
E --> G["Enable force-push protection"]

prompt: Clones of the `web-frontend` repo now take 12 minutes and `.git` weighs 3.4 GB. `git rev-list --objects --all | git cat-file --batch-check` sorted by size shows dozens of versions of `assets/demo-video.mp4` (each 80-150 MB) committed over the past year; the current version is still needed by the build. The team wants clones fast again and future versions of that file handled sensibly. What is the best approach?
options: Rewrite history with `git filter-repo` (or BFG) to strip the historical blobs, then track `*.mp4` with Git LFS going forward and have everyone re-clone
Add `assets/demo-video.mp4` to `.gitignore` and commit a deletion; the old blobs will be pruned on the next `git gc`
Run `git gc --aggressive --prune=now` on the server so the repository is repacked and the old video versions are compressed away
Tell developers to use `git clone --depth 1` and leave the history as it is
optionNotes: Correct: only a history rewrite removes the blobs from the object store, and LFS keeps future versions as small pointers with the binaries stored out of band.
Deleting and ignoring the file leaves every historical version reachable from old commits, so `gc` will not prune anything and clone size is unchanged.
Repacking cannot shrink objects that are still reachable; large binaries barely delta-compress, so the repository stays roughly the same size.
Shallow clones hide the problem for some workflows but break `git log`, bisect, and many CI tools, and the repository keeps growing with each new video commit.
explanation: Reachable objects are never garbage collected, so the historical video blobs only disappear if history is rewritten to exclude them. Moving the file to Git LFS afterwards means future revisions store a small pointer in Git and the binary in the LFS store, keeping clones fast.
example:
git filter-repo --path assets/demo-video.mp4 --invert-paths
git lfs install
git lfs track 'assets/*.mp4'
git add .gitattributes assets/demo-video.mp4
git commit -m 'Track demo video with LFS'
git push --force --all origin
# everyone: re-clone; git count-objects -vH to confirm size
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["3.4 GB .git, slow clones"] --> B["Find large blobs: rev-list + cat-file"]
B --> C["git filter-repo strips historical versions"]
C --> D["git lfs track for future versions"]
D --> E["Force push, team re-clones"]
F["gitignore or gc alone"] -.->|"blobs still reachable"| A

prompt: A feature branch was merged into `main` with a merge commit `e4f5a6b`, and production now throws errors traced to that feature. You must roll `main` back today without rewriting history because the branch is shared and protected. Running `git revert e4f5a6b` fails with `error: commit e4f5a6b is a merge but no -m option was given`. What is the correct fix?
options: Run `git revert -m 1 e4f5a6b`, which reverts to the first parent (the `main` side) and undoes everything the feature branch brought in
Run `git revert -m 2 e4f5a6b` so that the feature branch's side of the merge is kept as the mainline
Run `git reset --hard e4f5a6b~1` and push with `--force-with-lease` to remove the merge from `main`
Revert each individual commit from the feature branch with `git revert <sha>` one at a time, newest first
optionNotes: Correct: `-m 1` picks parent 1 (the `main` tip before the merge) as the mainline, so the revert produces a commit that removes the feature's changes.
Parent 2 is the feature branch tip; choosing it would instead undo the commits that were on `main` before the merge, which is the opposite of what is wanted.
This rewrites shared, protected history; the protection rules will reject the force push and collaborators would have to reset their clones.
This works only if the branch had few commits and no merges of its own; reverting the merge with `-m 1` achieves the same result in one atomic commit.
explanation: A merge commit has two parents, so Git needs to know which side is the mainline to compute the inverse diff. `-m 1` treats the first parent (the branch you merged into) as the baseline, so the resulting revert commit removes the feature's changes. Note that re-merging the same branch later requires reverting the revert, since Git now considers those commits already merged.
example:
git log --oneline -1 e4f5a6b
# e4f5a6b Merge branch 'feature/pricing' into main
git revert -m 1 e4f5a6b
git push origin main
# later, to bring the fixed feature back:
# git revert <sha-of-the-revert-commit>  then re-merge
diagram:
flowchart LR
P1["parent 1: main before merge"] --> M["merge e4f5a6b"]
P2["parent 2: feature tip"] --> M
M --> R["revert -m 1 (mainline = parent 1)"]
R --> S["main without feature changes"]
X["-m 2 would undo the main side instead"] -.-> M

prompt:
You run `git push origin feature/search` and get:
`! [rejected] feature/search -> feature/search (non-fast-forward)`
`hint: Updates were rejected because the tip of your current branch is behind its remote counterpart.`
A teammate confirms they pushed a small fix to the same branch this morning. What is the correct next step?
options: Run `git pull --rebase origin feature/search` (or `git fetch` then `git rebase origin/feature/search`), resolve any conflicts, and push again
Run `git push --force origin feature/search` so your local branch replaces the remote one
Delete the remote branch with `git push origin --delete feature/search` and push yours fresh
Run `git reset --hard origin/feature/search` and redo your changes on top
optionNotes: Correct: integrating the teammate's commit first makes your branch a descendant of the remote tip, so the push becomes a fast-forward.
This discards the teammate's fix from the remote branch; the rejection is Git protecting exactly that commit.
Deleting and re-pushing has the same effect as a force push: the teammate's commit is lost from the remote.
A hard reset throws away your own local commits; you would have to recover them from the reflog and redo the work needlessly.
explanation: A non-fast-forward rejection means the remote branch has commits your local branch does not contain. Fetch and rebase (or merge) the remote changes into your branch, then push; both histories are preserved and no force is needed.
example:
git pull --rebase origin feature/search
# Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/search.
git push origin feature/search
# or, to make this the default for pulls:
git config --global pull.rebase true
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["git push rejected: non-fast-forward"] --> B["Remote has commits you lack"]
B --> C["git pull --rebase origin branch"]
C --> D{"Conflicts?"}
D -->|"yes"| E["resolve, git rebase --continue"]
D -->|"no"| F["git push succeeds"]
E --> F
G["git push --force"] -.->|"drops teammate's commit"| B

prompt: A CI job for the `platform` repo fails at checkout with `fatal: remote error: upload-pack: not our ref 7d3e9f0` followed by `Fetched in submodule path 'libs/common', but it did not contain 7d3e9f0`. The last merged PR bumped the `libs/common` submodule pointer. Adding `git submodule update --init --recursive --force` to the CI script will resolve this failure.
explanation: The error means the superproject references a submodule commit that does not exist on the submodule's remote, almost always because the developer committed inside `libs/common` and updated the pointer but never pushed the submodule's commit. No checkout flag can fetch a commit the server does not have; the fix is to push the missing commit in the submodule repo (or point the superproject at a commit that exists).
example:
# in the developer's clone of libs/common
git -C libs/common log --oneline -1     # 7d3e9f0 exists locally
git -C libs/common push origin HEAD:main # push it so the remote has it
# guard against repeats in the superproject:
git config --global push.recurseSubmodules check
diagram:
flowchart TD
A["Dev commits in libs/common"] --> B["Superproject pointer set to 7d3e9f0"]
B --> C["Superproject pushed, submodule commit not pushed"]
C --> D["CI fetches submodule: not our ref"]
D --> E["Fix: push commit in submodule repo"]
F["push.recurseSubmodules=check blocks this"] -.-> C
